defect_cause:
Most probable cause [INFERENCE, strongly code-supported]: the adapter's post-shutdown lifecycle RPCs are unowned asynchronous work, not a running-status filter, cleanup-barrier deadlock, or demonstrated Brain refusal. Exact path: AttemptSettlementHandle.#publish -> AttemptSettlementRegistry.#deliver/#notify (src/task/attempt-settlement.ts:210-216,309-331) -> adapter snapshot callback (qualified-v2/brainstem/prime-extension/src/index.ts:1595-1639) -> observe's admission.callbackChain (1577-1585) -> observeWorkerAttempt -> await workerLifecycleRunner (1307) -> worker-lifecycle-bridge.ts:103-133 execFile Python -> worker_protocol.ingest_worker_lifecycle (1258-1422). The snapshot callback discards the promise using void Promise.resolve(observe(...)); #notify also has a void subscriber contract. Neither promise is owned by session disposal. AgentSession.#doDispose records session_exit at its START (agent-session.ts:4857-4864), then cancels/drains jobs; print-mode.ts:305 awaits that disposal, and main.ts:2359 calls postmortem.quit. pi-utils/src/postmortem.ts:703-719 ultimately calls process.exit. Consequently, being alive when a synchronous observer runs does not ensure survival through its later Python RPC.

Direct raw evidence: C:/Users/assas/.omp/profiles/canary-settlement/agent/sessions/-AppData-Local-Temp-omp-canary25-consumer-a/2026-09-19T15-57-19-957Z_01a0ba62-ead5-7189-a909-a446e04acda8.jsonl:12-19 contains observation revision1 at 15:57:29.424Z, worker-job-pending at 29.685Z, accepted receipt1 at 32.558Z, session_exit at 32.592Z, observation revision2 at 34.416Z, and revisions3/4 with cleanupState=settled AND releasePermitted=true at 34.645/34.652Z. Receipt1 took approximately 2.87 seconds after the binding journal. Thus settled observations definitely reached the extension callback, but entry into observeWorkerAttempt or completion of its subsequent RPC is not yet proven. These raw rows add detail missing from the abbreviated three-event journal summary.

The initial false/null receipt is expected after isolation-runner registers its pending cleanup before runSubprocess accepts a result. It is a legitimate earlier observation, not itself the defect. index.ts:1355's status!==running check is AFTER workerLifecycleRunner and accepted-receipt journaling; it suppresses only emitWorkerCompletion, never lifecycle ingest. Mapping revision3/4 cannot yield running: host snapshotOf makes releasePermitted imply resultAccepted. Host increments revision per publish; with only receipt1 accepted, revision3/4 cannot ordinarily fail revision<=lifecycleRevision. The Brain would accept an authenticated newer true/true receipt and release ownership (worker_protocol.py:1373-1408); no supplied evidence proves such a call occurred. The barrier promise replacement adds an asynchronous settlement hop but has no cycle: onRelease runs real cleanup, isolationRelease resolves, barrier settles, trackCleanups publishes. That sequence completed here. Do not rewrite outcome, change sequencing, bypass authentication, or equate ownership release with logical task completion.
defect_discriminating_experiment:
Run ONE RoughRabbit-style canary with the existing exact receipt guards and an instrumented, explicitly bounded post-cleanup observer drain. Do not delay publication on Brain availability. Capture a synchronous structured record at index.ts:1584 immediately inside callbackChain.then, before calling observeWorkerAttempt: event='second-brain.worker-lifecycle-chain-started', taskId, attemptId, nativeAttemptId, agentId, generation, sourceToolCallId/sourceIndex, observation.revision, admission.lifecycleRevision, status, executorSettled, cleanupComplete. This is the decisive missing line: it distinguishes 'snapshot observed but chain never entered' from admission refusal/RPC delay. Add explicit dropped records before the silent returns at 1581,1234,1245,1270/1272,1301, with reason and both incoming/bound identities. At 1307 log rpc-started; immediately after the await log rpc-returned with elapsedMs and the unmodified parsed result; retain existing accepted/rejected records and journal thrown exceptions too. Include resultAccepted/outcome and all identity fields in the existing observation record at 1596. Record host observer-drain-start/end/abandoned and immediately-before-quit timestamps in the same trace.

Interpretation: observed without chain-started => queue/lifetime loss before observeWorkerAttempt; chain-started plus dropped reason => exact admission/binding/revision refusal; rpc-started with no rpc-returned before quit => in-flight RPC abandoned, validating the leading hypothesis; rpc-returned ok=false => actual bridge/Brain refusal, distinguish transport error from protocol failure code; rpc-returned ok=true with missing durable row => capture the acknowledged database/home identity and investigate reading a different database or persistence, not the barrier. A newer true/true RPC accepted before bounded drain ends, with the durable sequence advancing, confirms the proposed ownership fix. Drain timeout MUST log abandonment and leave the durable held/quarantined row unchanged. Run the parent-approved bounded Brain-boundary regression before production; no test/build was run by this read-only reviewer.

one_shot_call_sites: src/task/structured-subagent.ts:487 forwards request.keepAlive to ExecutorOptions; :657-663 creates the attempt settlement handle; :685-696 invokes runIsolatedSubprocess for isolated requests. The one-shot branch is therefore a supported execution route, regardless of current external caller defaults.

src/task/isolation-runner.ts:514 (initial reviewed version) calls ensureIsolation before runSubprocess; :531 selects releaseBase only for keepAlive===false. This protects the worktree until post-run capture; it does NOT mean the execution owns no worktree.

src/task/executor.ts:3052-3057 implements the keepAlive=false lifecycle branch: disposeSession, unregister, releaseOwnedResources. disposeSession at :2982-2997 can register onCleanupDeferred(disposal), so even session cleanup may outlive a one-shot result.

src/task/isolation-runner.ts:644-665 (initial reviewed version) finally handles keepAlive=false: direct await cleanupHandle, or deferredCleanup.then(cleanupHandle) registered/tracked as late isolation cleanup; cleanupHandle at :392-397 calls cleanupIsolation(handle). Thus one-shot isolated executions concretely reach real native cleanup and may have cleanup beyond the visible result.
src/task/executor.ts:4120-4243 tracks late abort/session/owner-job work via cleanupDeferrals and onCleanupDeferred; those mechanisms are not restricted to keep-alive executions.

Classifier conclusion: an isolated one-shot must be required BEFORE resource acquisition because this route will acquire an isolation handle. Merely switching the current hard-coded classifier route from deferred to one-shot with the existing pre-acquisition {isolationResources:0, registeredCleanupWork:0} would incorrectly classify it none. Current host wiring conservatively classifies all runIsolatedSubprocess invocations required, including one-shot; do not replace that with a blanket one-shot exemption. A genuinely resource-free one-shot may still be none.
review_findings: P1 — Initial reviewed isolation-runner.ts:455-460 and :662-665 resolve isolationRelease in finally even if cleanupHandle/cleanupIsolation rejects; :490-491 then translates the signal into settleBarrier(ok:true). worktree.ts:617-648 correctly propagates isoStop/removal failures, but the new wiring erases that failure. finalizeSubagentLifecycle's releaseOwnedResources catches/logs onRelease errors (executor.ts:3005-3009), so this is a concrete false-release path, not just a misleading log. The parent subsequently added await cleanupHandle after isolationRelease; that addresses the rejected-cleanup case, but was not tested by this reviewer.

P1 — Retained-workspace capture failure remains a separate false-success path: releaseIsolation sets retainWorkspace=true on capture error; its finally runs cleanupHandle, which skips cleanupIsolation for retained handles, then resolves the signal. At the latest read, the parent's new retained-workspace branch only logs cleanup:skipped and returns successfully (isolation-runner.ts:396-403). Awaiting that memoized successful promise does not prove teardown; this branch must fail the cleanup proof, preserving recovery artifacts.

P1/P2 — Initial reviewed isolation-runner.ts:653-660 leaves the canonical barrier pending forever on deferred one-shot cleanup: it re-registers resource='isolation-handle' with deferredCleanup.then(cleanupHandle), but AttemptSettlementHandle.trackCleanups skips duplicate pending resource names at attempt-settlement.ts:141. That chain never resolved/rejected isolationRelease, the source for the original barrier. The parent subsequently changed this branch to settle the original barrier from the real deferred chain. Keep one registration and one authoritative terminal path; avoid retaining the unused unresolved deferred promise.

Identity answer: the CURRENT HOST WIRING closes over requirement.barrier and passes that exact promise to trackCleanups, so its dispatch-to-settlement object continuity is real. The module-wide claim is stronger than what the API enforces: exported createCleanupBarrier always constructs a new object for the same identity; releaseWhenProven accepts it without registry-membership validation. I1/I2 test only repeated barrierFor calls, not an independently constructed alternate barrier. The bare colon-concatenated barrierKey also admits distinct identity-tuple collisions. No second production factory caller was found; distinguish exported-contract weakness from an observed host bypass.

P2 — New releaseWhenProven at cleanup-barrier.ts:221 and releaseEligible at :288 have a check/use gap: `await revalidate()` yields even when revalidate returns boolean. A cancellation/new-generation microtask queued during revalidation can execute before permit. Allowing an async permit can add another gap if mutation occurs after its own await. I8 merely returns true/false in separate calls; it does not exercise this race. These helpers currently have no production callers outside tests, so this is a latent API defect, not the cause of RoughRabbit's missing receipt.

P2 — Required-to-none is not structurally prohibited: call classifyCleanupRequirement('one-shot', identity, {isolationResources:1,registeredCleanupWork:0}), then again with the SAME identity and zero counts; the second call returns none without checking the existing required barrier. assertNoDowngrade is an optional exported helper used only in its test. O5 constructs two different route identities and explicitly invokes that helper; it does not prove the classifier cannot downgrade. Current host's hard-coded deferred route and required check prevent this particular downgrade in runIsolatedSubprocess.

P2 — The barrier's identity is not the native execution identity: isolation-runner initially uses attemptId=opts.agentId, generation=0, while the dispatcher creates native attemptId like 32568:1:RoughRabbit and generation=1. Re-entering the API with the same agent label would retrieve a previously resolved barrier before new cleanup. Production fresh-name allocation reduces exposure, but the new global registry should key the authoritative settlement attempt/generation, not an agent label plus a constant. Copy/freeze the identity so later caller mutation cannot alter a registered barrier's meaning.

Qualification scope: read all four host-patch files, totaling B1-B12 (12), I1-I10 plus negative-return case (11), O1-O5 (5), and normalization (4) = 32 gates. None invokes runIsolatedSubprocess or actual cleanupIsolation; I5 supplies settleBarrier({ok:false}) directly rather than injecting a native cleanup failure through the real wiring. Therefore these gates cannot establish the wiring's fail-closed behavior, retained-workspace behavior, real identity propagation, late one-shot completion, or the Brain RPC disposal boundary. They were read, not executed.
